content: A total of 378 suggestions were submitted, with approximately 63% in English, 22% in French, 7% in Spanish, 6% in Chinese, 2% in Arabic, and none in Russian. Quantitative data analysis focused on the 20 interventions that were ranked most highly in three categories: (a) Essential everywhere (for all 86 interventions and for the 67 clinical interventions only), (b) Essential in certain geographic areas only, and (c) Unsuitable everywhere within school health services (SHS). Clinical interventions were defined as those requiring delivery or supervision by a health worker (n=60) or those that could be delivered by a health worker or delegated to a teacher with health-worker support or supervision (n=7). The analysis examined similarities and differences across WHO regions and respondents’ professions. The top 20 Essential everywhere interventions (both overall and clinical-only) were mapped to specific WHO programmatic areas (PAs) that support them. The 378 write-in interventions were translated into English when necessary and categorized under 16 health areas. Suggestions that duplicated one of the interventions detailed in the first 86 questions were removed unless multiple respondents emphasized their critical importance. The interventions were organized under the 16 questionnaire health areas, and subgroups were created to reflect emerging themes. Interventions were highlighted if they were suggested by many (6–8) or several (4–5) respondents. Survey respondents ranged in age from 25 to 81 years, with a mean and median age of 51 years. They represented 81 nationalities, with the most common being the Philippines (n=56), the United States (42), China (38), the United Kingdom (26), Australia (18), Canada (13), India (13), South Africa (13), Tunisia (13), Germany (10), Jordan (9), and Sweden (9). Additional sociodemographic characteristics of respondents were self-reported. The interventions ranked most highly as Essential everywhere in SHS were primarily in the areas of health promotion and health education. The top five specific interventions were: promotion of personal hygiene and handwashing with soap (80%), provision of sexual and reproductive health education (75%), promotion of health literacy (73%), health education about nutrition (73%), and promotion of oral health care (70%). However, five of the top seven interventions in this category were among the first six questions of the questionnaire, raising the possibility of response bias (e.g., initially affirmative responses to all questions, followed by more nuanced distinctions in later responses). To address this, Essential everywhere rankings of clinical interventions were also examined separately. Clinical interventions ranked most highly as Essential everywhere were in the areas of immunization, screening, assessment, and general care. Interventions ranked as Essential in certain geographic areas only addressed diverse conditions with limited geographic range due to disease prevalence, population characteristics, resources, ecology, and/or climate. The top five specific interventions in this category were: administration of immunizations recommended for children in certain regions (49%), provision and promotion of insecticide-treated bed nets (48%), administration of immunizations recommended for children in high-risk populations (44%), mass drug administration (38%), and promotion of sunscreen use to prevent sunburn and skin cancer (27%). Interventions ranked as Unsuitable everywhere in SHS were primarily in the category of noncommunicable disease screening, although specific interventions from other health-care categories (e.g., general care, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, injury prevention, and immunization) also ranked highly. The top five specific interventions in this category were: screening for hypertension (14%), administration of over-the-counter and prescribed medications (13%), and screening for diabetes (12%), scoliosis (12%), and other chronic conditions that may be undiagnosed (12%). Notably, the five interventions ranked most highly as Unsuitable everywhere were categorized this way by only 12–14% of respondents, while 2–3 times that proportion of respondents ranked each of these same interventions as Essential everywhere or Essential in certain geographic areas only. Four-fifths (81%) of the interventions in the questionnaire were ranked as Unsuitable everywhere by only 0–4% of respondents. There were no significant differences in the results by WHO region or by the profession of the respondent. Approximately half of the 378 write-in suggestions fell into the categories of health promotion, health education, and other aspects of health-promoting schools (HPS), with most in the latter category. The remaining suggestions primarily related to assessment, general care, noncommunicable conditions, and mental health care. Six interventions were suggested by many (6–8) respondents: health education about the safe use of technology/Internet; collaboration with school staff in multidisciplinary health services and classroom work; support for adequate and safe water and sanitation; early screening of students’ physical, behavioral, developmental, and learning needs; occupational therapy at all levels of the support continuum; and specific nutrition interventions, such as referral, support, and management for moderate and severe acute malnutrition or for overweight and obesity. The survey of expert opinion successfully collected meaningful data on the suitability of potential SHS interventions from a large and diverse sample of experts. Responses to all interventions listed in the questionnaire were generally favorable, and no interventions received overwhelmingly negative responses. The high overall ranking of health promotion and education interventions as Essential everywhere indicates that these are considered very important roles for health workers to perform within a school setting. The clinical interventions that ranked most highly as Essential everywhere were in the areas of immunization and mass drug administration, screening, assessment, and general care. Similarly, the most common write-in suggestions were in the areas of health education, other aspects of HPS, and screening and care for noncommunicable conditions.
